title: posts on Truth Social that Canada used AI for a television ad
description_short: posts on Truth Social that Canada used AI for a television ad
description_medium: President Trump posts on Truth Social that Canada used AI for a television ad that used audio from a 1987 address of President Ronald Reagan denouncing tariffs. The Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute later recommended everyone to watch the full unedited address on the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library YouTube account
description_long: In October 2025, Trump posted on Truth Social that Canada had used artificial intelligence in a television advertisement featuring Ronald Reagan’s criticism of tariffs. The advertisement used audio from a 1987 Reagan address opposing tariffs, and the Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute urged people to watch the complete, unedited speech. The dispute escalated during an already tense U.S.–Canada trade relationship: the linked coverage says the White House ended trade talks after the advertisement aired and Trump announced an increase in tariffs on Canadian goods. His assertion that the ad used AI was a public accusation; the supplied material establishes the use of Reagan’s recorded speech but does not show that the advertisement itself was generated or altered with AI. The incident brought a past Republican president’s trade views into a current dispute over Canadian advertising and U.S. tariffs. The sources supplied for this record do not give the size or effective date of the tariff increase, explain how negotiations changed afterward, or establish whether the ad’s production used AI. Those details are needed to describe the trade consequences or verify the central accusation.
organization_tags: Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute

title: Trump self-deals, lies and seems to fall asleep in meetings. The media treats it all as ‘priced in’ | Margaret Sullivan
description_short: Trump self-deals, lies and seems to fall asleep in meetings. The media treats it all as ‘priced in’ | Margaret Sullivan
description_medium: Guardian columnist Margaret Sullivan argued that major news outlets had normalized controversies in Trump’s second term, treating them as routine rather than pursuing sustained coverage. She cited his Iran-war statements, self-dealing allegations, apparent drowsiness in meetings, changes to the Kennedy Center and White House, and voting-rights disputes. These are examples in an opinion column, not independently adjudicated findings.
description_long: In a May 22, 2026 opinion column, Guardian media writer Margaret Sullivan argued that mainstream outlets were treating Trump’s second-term controversies as ordinary—“Trump being Trump”—instead of sustaining attention on them. She cited his Iran-war statements, claims about the war’s success, apparent sleep during meetings, alleged self-dealing and use of the Justice Department, as well as changes involving the Kennedy Center, the White House East Wing and voting rights for Black Americans. Sullivan contrasted this coverage with how she believed similar developments would have been treated before Trump’s presidency, and questioned whether the press was applying consistent standards. The article is an argument about media attention and normalization; it does not independently document each allegation or quantify how much coverage outlets gave to each issue. Its examples are presented as the columnist’s assessment of the political moment. The entry can therefore summarize Sullivan’s critique, but should not turn the column into proof that every listed allegation occurred as characterized or that news organizations deliberately suppressed coverage. A separate comparison of outlet coverage would be needed to assess that broader claim.

title: calls on Republicans to get rid of the filibuster rule requiring 60
description_short: President Trump calls on Republicans to get rid of the filibuster rule requiring 60 members to approve legislation, in an effort to end the government shutdown
description_medium: During the federal shutdown’s 30th day, Trump urged Senate Republicans to eliminate the filibuster so they could pass a funding bill with a simple majority. The rule generally requires 60 votes; Republicans held 53 Senate seats. Majority Leader John Thune opposed changing it. The dispute occurred as millions faced a possible loss of food assistance, though a federal judge blocked the administration from halting SNAP payments.
description_long: On October 31, 2025, with the federal shutdown entering its 30th day, Trump urged Senate Republicans to use the “nuclear option” and abolish the filibuster. The Senate rule generally requires 60 of 100 senators to advance most legislation; Republicans held 53 seats, so ending the rule would have let them pass a funding bill without Democratic votes. Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s spokesperson said his opposition to changing the filibuster remained unchanged. The shutdown had begun on October 1 and disrupted federal services. The BBC reported that more than 40 million people could lose access to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program if the shutdown continued into the weekend. A federal judge in Rhode Island had blocked the administration from stopping that food aid, ruling that the proposed halt was likely unlawful. Trump’s call was a proposal to change Senate procedure as part of the shutdown standoff; the report does not say the filibuster was abolished or that his request succeeded. The immediate stakes included negotiations over federal funding and food assistance, while the Senate’s response and shutdown outcome remained separate questions.

title: Trump: UAE restores power to Barakah nuclear plant after drone strike, says IAEA – as it happened

description_medium: The International Atomic Energy Agency said the United Arab Emirates had restored off-site power to a unit at the Barakah nuclear plant after a drone strike on Sunday. title: July Jobs Report: Economy Sheds 23,000 Jobs, Worst Since Pandemic
description_short: July Jobs Report: Economy Sheds 23,000 Jobs, Worst Since Pandemic
description_medium: The July 2026 U.S. jobs report recorded a net loss of 23,000 jobs, while analysts had expected an increase of about 80,000. The Bureau of Labor Statistics revised May and June payroll growth down by a combined 103,000. The BBC said losses were concentrated in local-government education and retail. The report describes labor-market data but does not establish a cause tied to Trump.
description_long: The U.S. employment report for July 2026 showed a net loss of 23,000 jobs, compared with analysts’ expectation of about 80,000 new jobs. The Bureau of Labor Statistics also revised May and June payroll growth down by a combined 103,000, indicating that hiring had been weaker over the summer than earlier estimates suggested. The BBC reported that losses were concentrated in local-government education and retail. Economists said the weaker figures could reduce pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, and U.S. markets opened higher after the report as investors considered the prospect of fewer rate increases. The employment report is a snapshot of payroll changes and revisions; by itself it does not identify why jobs declined or establish that a president’s policy caused the change. The supplied account gives no evidence tying the July figures to a specific Trump action. Its economic subject also does not fit the available canonical categories for political, rights, security or environmental harms. A separate source would be needed to connect the labor-market report to a specific policy or consequence in this timeline.
